title: Polymorphism
body:
"Many forms." One call, and which code runs is decided by the actual type of the object at
run time rather than by the declared type in the source.

```java
for (Shape s : shapes) {
    s.draw();          // Circle.draw, Square.draw, Triangle.draw
}                      // this loop never mentions any of them
```

That loop is the point of the whole idea: it does not change when a fourth shape is added.
The [[Interface]] is fixed, the [[Implementation]] varies, and the calling code was written
against the interface, so new variants slot in without editing existing code. Together with
[[Inheritance]] this is what "extensibility" means in the
[[Object Oriented Approach|OO benefits list]].

It is also a [[Coupling and Cohesion]] tool. Without it, the loop is a chain of
`if (s instanceof Circle) ... else if ...`, and every one of those chains has to be found and
edited for every new type. Polymorphism moves that decision into one place: the type itself.

**Overriding versus overloading.** Overriding is this: a subclass replaces a superclass
method, and the choice is made at run time by the object's real type. Overloading is several
methods with the same name and different parameter lists, resolved at compile time by the
argument types. Only the first is polymorphism in the sense the course means, and confusing
them is the standard exam trap.

See [[Classes]], [[Object]], [[OOD]], and [[Java]], where every non-final method is
polymorphic by default (the opposite of C++, where it needs `virtual`).

**Not to be confused with [[Parametric Polymorphism]]**, which is the same word for
a different mechanism: one implementation that works for every type, resolved at compile time,
where this note's sense is many implementations resolved at run time. [[Java]] has both, and
`List<T>` is the other one. That note carries the comparison table.
